text: Layered architecture with presentation, domain, and data access layers.
expected_response: Layered architecture organizes code into horizontal tiers—presentation, domain logic, and data access—where each layer depends only on the layer directly below it. This enforces separation of concerns and makes it easier to replace or refactor individual layers independently.

text: N-tier architecture for clear separation across UI, service, and persistence.
expected_response: N-tier architecture distributes responsibilities across distinct logical tiers such as UI, business service, and persistence. Each tier communicates through well-defined interfaces, enabling independent development, testing, and scaling of each tier.

text: Hexagonal architecture to isolate domain from infrastructure concerns.
expected_response: Hexagonal architecture places the domain model at the center, surrounded by ports that define how the application communicates with the outside world. Infrastructure concerns like databases and HTTP are pushed to adapters on the boundary, keeping the core logic free of external dependencies.

text: Ports and adapters for dependency inversion around domain core.
expected_response: Ports and adapters applies dependency inversion so the domain core defines interfaces (ports) that external systems implement through adapters. This ensures business logic remains testable and independent of any particular framework, database, or transport mechanism.

text: Microservices decomposition by bounded contexts and independent deployability.
expected_response: Microservices architecture decomposes a system along bounded context boundaries so each service owns its data and logic. This enables independent deployment, allowing teams to release, scale, and evolve services without coordinating across the entire system.

text: Service mesh and API gateway concerns in microservice ecosystems.
expected_response: In microservice ecosystems, a service mesh handles cross-cutting concerns like mutual TLS, retries, and observability at the infrastructure layer. An API gateway provides a unified entry point for external clients, managing routing, authentication, and rate limiting.

text: Event-driven architecture with pub/sub and asynchronous integration.
expected_response: Event-driven architecture uses asynchronous message passing via publish-subscribe channels so producers and consumers are decoupled in time and space. This approach improves scalability and resilience by allowing services to react to events independently without direct synchronous calls.

text: Message broker based event choreography between services.
expected_response: Event choreography uses a message broker to coordinate workflows across services without a central orchestrator. Each service listens for relevant events and reacts by emitting its own events, creating a decentralized flow that reduces single points of failure.

text: CQRS separates command writes from query reads for scaling.
expected_response: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) uses distinct models for write operations and read operations. By separating these concerns, each side can be optimized and scaled independently—write models for consistency and read models for throughput.

text: Combine CQRS with event sourcing for auditability and temporal queries.
expected_response: Pairing CQRS with event sourcing stores every state change as an immutable event, providing a complete audit trail. This enables temporal queries that reconstruct state at any point in time and supports rebuilding read models from the event log.

text: Monolith architecture can simplify operations for early-stage products.
expected_response: A monolithic architecture deploys the entire application as a single unit, which simplifies development, testing, and operations when the team and codebase are small. This approach avoids the overhead of distributed systems and is often the right starting point for early-stage products.

text: Modular monolith to keep strong boundaries without distributed complexity.
expected_response: A modular monolith organizes code into well-defined modules with strict interface boundaries while deploying as a single unit. This preserves the simplicity of monolithic operations while maintaining the encapsulation benefits that make future service extraction feasible.

text: Layered system architecture for enterprise apps with clear boundary contracts.
expected_response: Enterprise layered architectures define explicit contracts between each layer, typically through interfaces or DTOs. These boundary contracts ensure that changes in one layer—such as switching a data access implementation—do not cascade into adjacent layers.

text: Use layered architecture to isolate controllers, services, and repositories.
expected_response: Isolating controllers, services, and repositories into distinct layers ensures that HTTP handling, business logic, and data persistence are independently testable. Each layer has a clear responsibility, preventing business rules from leaking into the presentation or persistence tier.

text: Hexagonal architecture keeps core domain independent from DB and HTTP adapters.
expected_response: In hexagonal architecture, the core domain defines port interfaces that database and HTTP adapters implement externally. This means the domain can be fully tested in isolation using in-memory fakes, and infrastructure technologies can be swapped without changing business logic.

text: Ports-and-adapters architecture enables swapping infrastructure implementations.
expected_response: Ports-and-adapters makes infrastructure implementations interchangeable by having the domain depend only on abstract port definitions. Whether switching from PostgreSQL to DynamoDB or from REST to gRPC, only the adapter layer changes while the core application remains untouched.

text: Microservice architecture for independently deployable bounded contexts.
expected_response: Microservice architecture aligns each service with a bounded context from domain-driven design, giving it ownership of its own data store and deployment lifecycle. This independence allows teams to ship features, choose technology stacks, and scale services without cross-team coordination.

text: In microservices architecture, API gateway and service discovery are key concerns.
expected_response: An API gateway aggregates and routes external traffic to internal services, handling cross-cutting concerns like auth and rate limiting. Service discovery enables services to locate each other dynamically, which is essential as instances scale up, down, or move across hosts.

text: Event-driven system architecture using asynchronous pub-sub communication.
expected_response: An event-driven system with asynchronous pub-sub communication allows producers to emit events without waiting for consumers to process them. This temporal decoupling improves system resilience and enables horizontal scaling of consumers independently from producers.

text: Event choreography architecture with brokers decouples service interactions.
expected_response: In event choreography, a message broker mediates interactions so services never call each other directly. Each service reacts to events it cares about and publishes outcomes, creating loosely coupled workflows that are easier to extend without modifying existing services.

text: CQRS architecture separates command model from query model for scaling.
expected_response: CQRS architecture maintains separate data models for commands (writes) and queries (reads), allowing each to use storage and schemas optimized for its access patterns. This separation is particularly valuable when read and write workloads have very different scaling characteristics.

text: Architectural CQRS pattern with read replicas and write consistency boundary.
expected_response: CQRS with read replicas directs queries to eventually consistent replicas while writes go through a strongly consistent primary. This defines a clear consistency boundary where the write side guarantees correctness and the read side optimizes for low-latency, high-throughput queries.

text: Monolithic architecture can simplify deployment and observability in small teams.
expected_response: For small teams, a monolithic architecture consolidates deployment into a single artifact and provides straightforward observability through unified logging and tracing. This reduces operational overhead and lets the team focus on delivering features rather than managing infrastructure.

text: Architectural choice of modular monolith before microservices migration.
expected_response: Starting with a modular monolith establishes clean domain boundaries and well-defined module interfaces before introducing distributed complexity. When the need for independent scaling or deployment arises, modules can be extracted into microservices along pre-existing boundaries.

text: Layered architecture clarifies boundaries between API, service, and repository tiers.
expected_response: By structuring code into API, service, and repository tiers, layered architecture makes each tier's responsibility explicit. This clarity simplifies onboarding, testing, and refactoring since developers know exactly where request handling, business logic, and data access belong.

text: N-tier system architecture supports independent scaling by logical tier.
expected_response: N-tier architecture allows each logical tier to be deployed and scaled independently based on its resource demands. For example, the presentation tier can scale horizontally to handle traffic spikes while the data tier scales vertically for write throughput.

text: Hexagonal architecture keeps application core isolated behind ports.
expected_response: Hexagonal architecture shields the application core by exposing only port interfaces to the outside world. All interactions—whether from a web controller, a CLI, or a message queue—pass through these ports, ensuring the core remains agnostic to delivery mechanisms.

text: Adapters implement infrastructure concerns while domain remains framework-agnostic.
expected_response: In hexagonal architecture, adapters encapsulate all framework and infrastructure specifics—ORM mappings, HTTP serialization, message queue clients—behind port contracts. The domain layer depends only on these abstract ports, keeping it testable and portable across technology changes.

text: Microservices architecture enables team autonomy and independent release cadence.
expected_response: Microservices give each team full ownership of their service's lifecycle, from development through deployment. Teams can choose their own release cadence, technology stack, and scaling strategy without blocking or being blocked by other teams.

text: Service boundaries in microservices align with bounded contexts and ownership.
expected_response: Aligning microservice boundaries with bounded contexts ensures each service has a cohesive domain model and clear data ownership. This prevents shared database anti-patterns and makes service contracts explicit, reducing coupling between teams and codebases.

text: Event-driven architecture propagates state changes with asynchronous events.
expected_response: Event-driven architecture propagates state changes as immutable events that downstream consumers process asynchronously. This decouples the producer from the timing and number of consumers, enabling reactive systems that scale and evolve independently.

text: Pub-sub architecture allows multiple consumers per event stream.
expected_response: Publish-subscribe architecture fans out each event to all subscribed consumers, allowing multiple systems to react to the same event independently. This enables use cases like updating a search index, sending notifications, and recording analytics from a single order-placed event.

text: CQRS architecture improves read throughput by separate read models.
expected_response: CQRS improves read throughput by maintaining denormalized read models tailored to specific query patterns. These read models can use optimized storage like search indices or materialized views, avoiding the joins and complexity of the normalized write model.

text: Command and query segregation reduces write-side complexity in scaling scenarios.
expected_response: By segregating commands from queries, the write side can focus purely on enforcing invariants and processing state transitions without being burdened by read optimization concerns. This focused responsibility reduces complexity and makes the write path easier to reason about under load.

text: Monolithic architecture often improves local developer productivity at early stage.
expected_response: At the early stage, a monolithic architecture lets developers run the entire system locally, debug across module boundaries easily, and refactor fearlessly with IDE support. This tight feedback loop accelerates iteration compared to coordinating across distributed services.

text: Modular monolith architecture maintains domain boundaries inside one deployable unit.
expected_response: A modular monolith enforces strict domain boundaries through module interfaces and access control within a single deployable artifact. This gives teams the encapsulation benefits of microservices while retaining the operational simplicity of a monolithic deployment.

text: Layered plus domain-driven boundaries can reduce accidental cross-layer coupling.
expected_response: Combining layered architecture with domain-driven boundaries creates both horizontal and vertical separation. Horizontal layers enforce technical responsibility, while vertical domain boundaries prevent unrelated business concerns from coupling through shared data structures or services.

text: Hexagonal architecture supports testing via fake adapters and contract tests.
expected_response: Hexagonal architecture enables fast, reliable testing by substituting real infrastructure adapters with in-memory fakes or mocks. Contract tests verify that real adapters conform to port interfaces, ensuring integration correctness without requiring the full infrastructure stack in every test run.

text: Microservices require observability, tracing, and resilient network patterns.
expected_response: Distributed microservices demand robust observability through structured logging, distributed tracing, and metrics aggregation. Resilient network patterns like circuit breakers, retries with backoff, and bulkheads are essential to prevent cascading failures across service boundaries.

text: Event-driven designs benefit from idempotent consumers and at-least-once handling.
expected_response: At-least-once delivery semantics mean consumers may receive duplicate events, so designing idempotent handlers is critical. Idempotent consumers use techniques like deduplication keys or upsert operations to ensure processing the same event multiple times produces the same result.

text: CQRS with materialized views accelerates read APIs under heavy load.
expected_response: Materialized views in a CQRS system pre-compute and store query results, enabling read APIs to serve responses directly without complex joins or aggregations. This dramatically reduces read latency under heavy load while the write side independently maintains consistency.

text: Monolith-first can defer distributed complexity until product-market fit.
expected_response: A monolith-first strategy defers the operational and cognitive overhead of distributed systems until the product has validated its market fit. This allows the team to iterate quickly on features and domain modeling before committing to service boundaries that are costly to change later.

text: Layered architecture enforces dependency direction from outer layers inward.
expected_response: Layered architecture enforces a strict dependency direction where outer layers (presentation, controllers) depend on inner layers (domain, services) but never the reverse. This ensures that core business logic remains stable and unaffected by changes in delivery mechanisms or UI frameworks.

text: Ports and adapters support replacing persistence technology with minimal domain impact.
expected_response: With ports and adapters, the persistence layer is an adapter behind a repository port defined by the domain. Migrating from one database technology to another only requires writing a new adapter that satisfies the existing port contract, leaving domain logic completely unchanged.

text: Microservice architecture should avoid distributed monolith anti-patterns.
expected_response: A distributed monolith occurs when microservices are tightly coupled through shared databases, synchronous call chains, or lock-step deployments. Avoiding this anti-pattern requires enforcing service autonomy, asynchronous communication, and independent data ownership from the start.

text: Event bus architecture improves extensibility for independently evolving features.
expected_response: An event bus enables new features to subscribe to existing event streams without modifying the producing services. This open-closed extensibility means the system grows by adding new consumers rather than changing established code paths, reducing regression risk.

text: CQRS write model consistency and read model eventual consistency trade-offs.
expected_response: CQRS introduces a trade-off where the write model guarantees strong consistency while read models are eventually consistent. Applications must design for this lag—using techniques like read-your-own-writes or optimistic UI updates—to maintain a good user experience despite propagation delay.

text: Modular monolith architecture can be stepping stone toward service extraction.
expected_response: A modular monolith with well-defined module boundaries and explicit inter-module contracts serves as a natural stepping stone to microservices. When a module needs independent scaling or deployment, it can be extracted into a service along its existing boundary with minimal restructuring.
